title: More budget never removes effort: the measure-order form of Gavish and Katriel's budget-monotonicity conjecture for periodic regulation
oneLine: In Gavish and Katriel's model of seasonal control, raising the yearly effort budget never makes it optimal to do less at any time of year; the paper proves this and shows exactly where it stops holding.
abstract: Many control problems share one shape: a stock (larvae, pests, a pool of susceptible people, a harvested population or a pollutant) is refilled by a seasonal inflow, decays naturally and is reduced by effort that removes a fixed fraction of what is present, continuously or in instantaneous pulses. With a fixed yearly effort budget the planner minimises the seasonally weighted average stock. Gavish and Katriel (Applied Mathematics & Optimization, 2026) conjectured that a larger budget never makes it optimal to do less at any time. This candidate proves the measure-order (weak) form of that conjecture: in their model, under their uniqueness assumption, the optimal effort assigned to every set of times is nondecreasing in the budget. Supports are nested, every pulse grows, and an optimal plan can be built incrementally. The strict inequality displayed in the source is false in general. The order survives caps on pulses and treatment rates; it can fail under seasonal prices or seasonal efficacy, and with finitely many dates under a nonlinear state cost (exact counterexamples, a sufficient price condition and an elasticity criterion are given). Under a dose budget with finitely many dates the problem becomes linear. The related vaccination conjecture (Conjecture 8 of Gavish and Katriel, Bulletin of Mathematical Biology, 2026) follows in measure form and pointwise except at a precisely described set of points. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Budget monotonicity (Theorem 1.1, proof): for every pair of budgets M1 ≤ M2 the optimal effort measures satisfy μ_M1(E) ≤ μ_M2(E) for every Borel set E of times, under Gavish and Katriel's uniqueness assumption, including pulses and nonsmooth data. Supports are nested, pulses grow and optimal levels fall at every time.
The strict inequality displayed in the source conjecture is false in general; the weak form is the one the source's prose and first formulation assert.

Limits (proofs and exact certificates): monotonicity survives caps on pulses and treatment rates; it can fail with seasonal prices or seasonal efficacy, including among all effort measures with one continuous price, and with finitely many dates under a quadratic state cost; a price-band sufficient condition holds for finitely many dates.
Dose budgets with finitely many dates make the problem linear: with a unique best date, the optimum below an eradication threshold is one campaign there (proof).

The vaccination density conjecture (Gavish and Katriel, Conjecture 8) holds in measure form and pointwise except where the density formula is undefined or uses a discontinuous derivative representative (proof).

narration: More budget never removes effort. An Evidence Press briefing. Many planning problems share one simple shape. Think of mosquito larvae, crop pests, people waiting to be vaccinated, or a harvested fish stock. A stock is refilled by a seasonal inflow, decays naturally, and is reduced by effort that removes a share of it, either steadily or in short pulses. With a fixed amount of effort each year, the planner wants the lowest seasonally weighted average stock. Gavish and Katriel worked out what the best plans look like, and conjectured that a bigger budget never makes it optimal to do less at any time of year. That is not obvious, because effort early in the year lowers the stock later, so extra money might in principle be better spent by moving effort between seasons. This release proves the conjecture in the form the authors describe in words. In their model, when the yearly budget rises, the optimal effort in every part of the year can only stay the same or grow. Treated seasons are nested, and no pulse ever gets smaller. So plans can be built step by step: if the budget goes up, add to the existing plan, and nothing already scheduled needs to be cancelled. The paper also shows where this stops. It survives limits on how much can be done at once. It can fail when effort is cheaper, or works better, in some seasons than in others; then extra budget can make it optimal to shrink one round. With fixed treatment dates, it can also fail when the cost of the stock is not proportional to its size. And if the budget counts doses rather than the share removed, the problem changes character, and the best plan is often a single campaign. A related conjecture by the same authors, about the timing of seasonal vaccination, also follows, apart from a narrow technical exception. The practical advice is to fix the unit of the budget first, and to check whether prices or efficacy vary with the season. These are mathematical results about a simple model, not field evidence. This is an anonymous, AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate, not peer reviewed or independently reproduced. Published on 21 October 2026, its paper and evidence are linked from the Evidence Press release page. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.

decisionObject.description: A proof that optimal periodic effort measures are ordered in the budget (the measure-order form of the Gavish–Katriel conjecture), with exact boundaries: prices, efficacy, nonlinear costs and dose budgets, and the vaccination Conjecture 8.
decisionObject.scope: Scalar linear periodic model S' = c − (δ + η)S with exponential pulses, linear weighted state cost and a budget of log-kill units, under the source's uniqueness assumption; price-band, elasticity and dose results only for finitely many treatment dates. Not an empirical claim about any intervention.
